rationale: A new assessment is written because the featured set changes and the incumbent's adopted assessment was incomplete: it carried no steelman and no per-claim treatments. GEO-C506 (surface salt on pyramid stone) is added to the featured set because the ledger now holds its own evidence record (GEO-E026, the proponents' taste-test statement) and a dedicated research item (GEO-R010, the missing bedrock comparator); it is the modern form of the salt argument and belongs beside GEO-C003 rather than hidden behind it. GEO-C903 stays unfeatured — its only evidence record was rejected — but the Iwawe model it describes is explained in prose because GEO-R009 makes it the cheapest test of the Andean branch. The case verdict stays unresolved and the load-bearing set is unchanged. Low-rung claims resting on a single uncontested weak proponent record (GEO-C002, GEO-C006, GEO-C013, GEO-C005) are regraded from unresolved to weakly_supported, since 'unresolved' implies a collision the ledger does not contain; GEO-C004 is regraded to provisionally_supported to separate the published observation (real, peer-reviewed) from its untested interpretation. The crux order now leads with the two tests that do not depend on contested sample custody: the blinded paleomagnetic survey (GEO-R011) and the Iwawe/piedras-cansadas desk check (GEO-R009), then the methods audit that decides how much provenance evidence constrains anything. The article drops assertions not in the ledger (currently funded research, researcher nationalities, a 1979 date), corrects 'nobody has looked' to what the ledger supports (the salt report is untraced to a medieval author), adds the binder shift from alkali geopolymer to calcium-silicate cement and what it does to the negatives, exposes the wrong-comparator problem in the salt argument, describes the proponents' checkable Iwawe model, and ends with a visible two-column what-would-change-our-mind list. All five plates are retained; the Rekhmire plate moves next to the mural discussion.
article:
At the granite quarries of Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, there is a block that tourists are invited to hit. The idea is charming: pick up one of the rounded dolerite stones that ancient workers supposedly used, strike the granite, and feel the past in your hands. Guides have been running this accidental experiment for decades. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever managed to reproduce one of the smooth, scooped depressions that cover the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. The stones bounce. The granite shrugs.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

Anecdotes like this prove nothing by themselves, and this one has never been systematically surveyed — nobody has counted the attempts, weighed the effort, or examined the test block for wear. But it points at the right question, which is not *who built the monuments* — nobody serious disputes that ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and ancient Andeans built Tiwanaku — but *how the hardest stone was worked*. The megalithic casting hypothesis gives a heterodox answer: some of it was not worked at all. It was made — mixed, moulded, and set in place, the way we make concrete — from crushed or gathered rock, a mineral binder, and chemistry that a Bronze Age society could plausibly command.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The idea has a serious pedigree and a disreputable neighbourhood. It was put in scientific form by the French materials chemist Joseph Davidovits, whose group has since published in peer-reviewed materials journals, and it has attracted at least one laboratory with no stake in the theory. It also circulates in a media ecosystem of lost civilisations and ancient high technology that this case has nothing to do with. Casting requires no aliens, no Atlantis, and no forgotten machines — only forgotten chemistry, which is a documented historical phenomenon. That is what makes it testable, and what makes the testing so far — real, contested, and short of decisive — worth laying out in full.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Any honest map of this dispute starts by steelmanning the orthodoxy, because the orthodoxy is strong.

The carved-and-transported account is not a guess. Quarries exist, with unfinished monuments still attached to bedrock — the Aswan obelisk itself is the most famous, abandoned mid-extraction after the granite cracked. Tools have been recovered in quantity. Worker settlements at Giza have been excavated. Experimental archaeologists have carved granite with dolerite and copper, slowly but genuinely. And modern geochemical provenancing has matched monument stone to specific quarries. The cleanest example is Stonehenge: immobile-trace-element analysis finds that fifty of fifty-two sarsens share a single geochemical profile, and Stone 58's signature directly matches the West Woods area about 25 km away — not a loose statistical resemblance but a match.

The conventional account's gaps are quantitative, not existential. It needs no miracle anywhere. What it needs, in a few specific places, is more time, more workers, or better technique than anyone has yet demonstrated. Those places are where this case lives.

## Where the anomalies actually are

Strip away everything anecdotal and the residue is small but real. It comes in three kinds: rates, ingredients, and the record.

### Rates

For a century the standard account of granite quarrying rested largely on Reginald Engelbach's 1922 report on the Aswan obelisk. Proponents characterise its experimental basis as a single self-conducted one-hour trial and a heuristic workforce estimate; that characterisation is theirs and has not yet been checked against the monograph, so hold it loosely. In 2023 a team finally produced a modern number: [photogrammetric measurement of granite removal with a dolerite pounder gave roughly 216 cubic centimetres per hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001} — a rate the authors themselves say speaks against pounders as the *sole* quarrying method. That is a peer-reviewed measurement, from a single team, and it is the most mainstream-legible item in the anomaly column.

Note carefully what it is evidence *for*. It stresses the orthodox timeline. It says nothing about casting: fire-setting, chisels, or simply more labour would each absorb the shortfall without a single mould. The same goes for the quarry's stranger features — [vertical shafts some five metres deep, described as too narrow for a worker to swing a pounder at their bottom]{claim=GEO-C006} — which have not been surveyed by anyone without a stake in the answer.

### Ingredients

The natron-route version of the hypothesis, developed by the researcher Marcell Fóti, starts from a well-documented fact: Egypt sat on [industrial-scale deposits of natron — the alkaline salt ancient glassmakers used as a flux — exploited from antiquity, with supply declining sharply in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. Natron plus heat plus silica gives waterglass, a mineral binder, and [the roughly 850 °C required was within reach of charcoal-and-bellows pyrotechnology]{claim=GEO-C010} — a point the ledger supports only through a proponent's citation of early glassmaking, though what is known of ancient metallurgy makes it hard to doubt. Crucible-scale heat, however, is not industrial-scale processing, and the natron papers concern glass and faience; they say nothing about stone. The proposed discovery story — that [long-used outdoor fire pits accidentally produce hardened artificial stone through ash chemistry]{claim=GEO-C013} — rests on one unattributed anecdote and has never been replicated.

All of this is necessary for casting and none of it is evidence of casting. Ingredients on the shelf do not make a cake.

### The record

The historical anchors are thinner still. Proponents report that when Caliph Al-Ma'mun's party forced its way into the Great Pyramid in the ninth century, it [found the interior chamber walls coated with a layer of salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — an odd thing for a sealed structure of dry quarried limestone to do, and an expected thing for stone that set wet with natron in it. But the only record of that report in this case is the proponents' own web page, and the report has not been traced to a primary Arabic source. It might dissolve on contact with one.

The modern version of the same argument — that [Great Pyramid stones carry surface salt that comparable natural limestone does not]{claim=GEO-C506} — currently rests on Davidovits tasting fragments on four visits between 1984 and 2003 and finding them salty, and on the observation that European cathedrals are not salt-encrusted. That is the wrong control. Cathedrals are different limestone in a different climate; the relevant comparator is unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock and quarry faces, which nobody in this record has tested. Salt also has mundane candidate origins — efflorescence from mortar, groundwater wicking, centuries of visitors — and a surface taste cannot distinguish any of them from salt bound in the bulk of the stone.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

Finally there is a picture. In the Tomb of Rekhmire an 18th-Dynasty mural shows a large casting operation — rows of crucibles tended by workers with poles. Egyptology reads it as bronze casting. Fóti argues that [the scale and apparatus depicted fit mineral or waterglass processing better than bronze work]{claim=GEO-C005}. That is an interpretive argument by a proponent that conventional Egyptology has not engaged; a serious re-reading would ask what residues or tools each interpretation predicts in the archaeological record, and go and look.

## The stone itself

Everything above is circumstantial. The case turns on what the monument stone is actually made of, and here two branches have very different records.

### Egypt: tested, and mostly failed

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The pyramid claim is that [some blocks of the Great Pyramid — not the core, but casing, tops, and backing blocks — are cast reconstituted limestone rather than quarried natural stone]{claim=GEO-C020}. Two laboratory results point that way. In 2006 a Drexel University group compared pyramid limestone under electron microscopy with six natural limestones from the area and reported microconstituents combining silicon, calcium, and magnesium "in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources", along with hydrated phases "not known to hydrate in nature" — while conceding that nature "could have — however unlikely — produced all the microstructures examined". In 2011 an overlapping team applied solid-state NMR to a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur and read it as Tura limestone grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel "formed by human intervention", perhaps with diatomaceous earth added.

Notice the second result quietly changes the recipe. Davidovits proposed an alkali-aluminosilicate geopolymer; the NMR study proposes a lime-pozzolan cement — the chemistry of a mortar, not of a geopolymer. That matters for how the negatives count.

And the negatives are substantial. Four independent petrographic examinations — petrography is the study of stone under a microscope, the geologist's basic tool — every one concluding natural limestone. Folk and Campbell, working across many blocks in the field, report sedimentary bedding, burrows, sharp cross-sections of clams and fragile worm tubes, ripple lamination, and calcite-filled tectonic fractures confined to individual blocks — features that geology produces and moulds do not. Harrell and Penrod examined the "Lauer sample", the pyramid-interior specimen proponents cite as their showcase, and found natural Mokattam limestone with "no evidence of the special textures and zeolite cement that must exist if the sample is concrete". Freestone and Middleton ran five techniques on a British Museum casing fragment and found no feature supporting an artificial origin; the cristobalite that Davidovits once treated as a synthetic marker turned out to be opal-CT, a normal sedimentary product. And Jana did the one thing nobody else in this literature has done: he examined casing stones side by side with natural Tura limestone *and* a genuine Davidovits-made geopolymer block. The silicon-rich spheres highlighted in 2006 appeared in casing stones and natural limestone alike. The geopolymer showed a binder heavily enriched in sodium, potassium, and aluminium that no casing stone showed. The artificial block had a smooth matrix with spherical air voids; the monument stone and the quarry stone shared a grainy texture with pores between the grains.

What keeps this exchange from being decisive is a fight over the samples themselves. Davidovits contends the piece his critics analysed was not the authentic Lauer sample — wrong thickness, missing phosphate coating — though Jana reports finding and mapping that very coating on the piece he received. Egypt's antiquities authority, for its part, states that no sampling permission was ever granted for the 2006 study and that its samples' origin is unknown. And Jana's decisive negative is a negative for the *alkali* recipe; it does not test the calcium-silicate binder of the 2011 NMR study, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which, at a few per cent by weight, might hide from bulk chemistry. That narrow residue — a low-percentage lime-pozzolan cement in some casing stones — is what survives on the Egyptian side.

### The Andes: one team, never rerun

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

At Pumapunku in Bolivia the laboratory evidence is the only kind from a disputed monument that supports casting outright. [Published SEM and petrographic analyses of the andesite report organic matter and microstructural features the authors argue natural volcanic stone should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}, and on that basis the claim is that [some andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku and Tiwanaku were geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021}. Those papers passed peer review in materials journals. They also come from one team — the Davidovits group — analysing one sample set whose chain of custody is contested, and no independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. Volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally, and the criteria for telling natural from artificial were never blind-tested.

The standing counter-evidence is a 1971 Bolivian Academy of Sciences study attributing Pumapunku's red sandstones to identifiable natural quarries. It is a provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other. The proponents' own current model is more specific than it used to be, and therefore more checkable: it holds that the andesite was cast from natural, uncrushed volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia, stored in a lakeshore deposit at Iwawe, and that the abandoned quadrangular blocks called *piedras cansadas* — "tired stones" — were not building material. Both the orthodox account and the proponents agree the andesite comes from Khapia, so quarry geochemistry cannot separate them; a lakeshore deposit and some abandoned blocks can. Reading the excavators' own description of that deposit is desk work.

### Can it be done at all?

The one rung of the ladder in decent shape is the humblest: [limestone can be reconstituted into large, hard blocks visually similar to natural stone with materials and temperatures available to ancient builders]{claim=GEO-C012}. Davidovits' institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, self-reported and never independently analysed; lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate gel at room temperature in the laboratory; and the geopolymer block Jana examined is, after all, a real artificial limestone. Feasibility is not occurrence. But it is not nothing either, and it is the reason this case is a question and not a fantasy.

## The ladder, and why it thins as it climbs

Notice the shape. At the bottom: observations, some solid, most unverified. In the middle: mechanism claims — the ingredients existed, the temperatures were reachable, the chemistry works. At the top: the claim that actually matters, that [at least one major megalithic monument, somewhere, contains man-made cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022}. Each rung is weaker than the one below, and evidence for a lower rung does not automatically climb. Natron in Egypt is well documented and proves nothing about pyramids. Feasibility is real and proves nothing about history.

The headline claim is existential — *at least one* monument — so it cannot be settled by averaging. Egypt has been tested with binder-aware methods and, in the recipe tested, failed. The Andes have been examined by one interested team and by nobody else. Neither branch has what a positive result needs: an independent laboratory, provenance-secure samples, criteria fixed in advance.

## The crux

Here is where the disagreement lives, and it is narrower than either camp usually admits.

The strongest conventional evidence class is provenance matching: monument stone chemically fingerprinted to a quarry. The casting hypothesis's most consequential reply is methodological — [that trace-element quarry-matching methods are blind to hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen, and so cannot by design tell carved quarry stone from stone cast using aggregate gathered at that same quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. Crushed rock keeps its metallic fingerprint. The narrow point is correct: portable XRF and ICP-MS do not see the light elements a binder is made of, and a quarry match is a quarry match, not a proof of carving. Even at Stonehenge, the West Woods result tells you where the sarsen came from, not how it was shaped.

But the reply reaches less far than its authors want. Fóti's own methods table lists NMR as blind to silicon and oxygen, when solid-state silicon NMR is exactly what the pro-casting Bent Pyramid study used. And the critique does not touch the direct petrography at all. Cast stone needs a binder; binders have signatures — bound water, alkali enrichment, textures geology does not produce. Jana's positive control demonstrates those signatures are plainly visible when present. A methods audit of the provenance literature is worth doing, and it would likely show that some "we found the quarry" conclusions have been stretched into "therefore carved" conclusions the chemistry cannot carry. It would not rescue a monument in which someone has looked directly for a binder and found none.

## What would change our mind

The strongest case for the hypothesis that this record does not answer is this: the revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for. The four negative Egyptian studies were built around the alkali recipe, and the one with a positive control used an alkali geopolymer as the control. A cement at five per cent by weight — exactly the kind the 2011 NMR study proposes and the 2010 laboratory work shows is easy to make — could sit inside a casing stone that reads as natural in every one of those tests. Nothing in the record rules that out, and the provenance critique means quarry matching cannot rule it out either.

The strongest case against is equally plain: every time monument stone has been examined directly for casting by anyone outside the proponent camp, it has read as natural — down to fossil worm tubes and tectonic fractures.

So here is what would move us.

- **Toward casting:** an independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku organic and microstructural findings on samples with a documented chain of custody; a provenance-secure Egyptian casing stone in which an independent lab finds a calcium-silicate cement absent from matched Tura limestone; a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many pyramid blocks finding a shared remanence aligned with the present field — something a block that set in place should carry regardless of recipe, and a quarried, rotated block should not.
- **Toward carving:** an independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy; a targeted test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure casing stone returning nothing; halite effloresc­ing from unworked Giza bedrock, which would retire the salt argument entirely; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be dressing debris or unrelated fill, with carved andesite blocks documented in transit from Khapia.

This case does not end in a verdict, because on the present record no honest verdict is available. It ends in a research agenda, much of it cheap. Read the Iwawe excavation report. Trace the salt story to a medieval author or drop it. Test whether the plateau's own bedrock effloresces salt. Audit which provenance studies can, and cannot, see a binder. Audit the restoration histories that could account for any surface anomaly. Replicate the quarrying rate. Re-read the Rekhmire mural with a metallurgist and a chemist in the same room. And design, at last, the blinded comparison of disputed monument stone against geologically matched natural rock, with the criteria written down before anyone looks.

The scoop marks at Aswan have waited a very long time for someone to measure them properly. The full agenda, with what each project would tell us, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis (GEO-C022) is existential — at least one monument — so the case verdict cannot be an average across branches. The Egyptian branch is the only one tested with binder-aware methods on monument stone, and in the recipe tested it failed: GEO-E018, GEO-E019, GEO-E021 and above all GEO-E020, whose genuine Davidovits-made positive control shows that an alkali-aluminosilicate binder is plainly visible when present and absent from every casing stone examined. What survives on the Egyptian side is narrower than the claim as originally stated: the calcium-silicate (C–S–H) binder of GEO-E017, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which GEO-E020's alkali-specific negative does not test, plus the GEO-E012 microconstituents, whose sample provenance is contested and whose distinguishing features GEO-E020 found in natural limestone too. The Andean branch (GEO-E006, GEO-E007) is one team, one sample set, contested custody, never independently rerun; the only counterweight, GEO-E008, is a 1971 provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other — an untested branch, not a genuine evidential collision. The proponents' methods critique (GEO-C030, GEO-E024) holds in its narrow form: light-element blindness is real for PXRF and ICP-MS and legitimately qualifies quarry-match reasoning such as GEO-E009, but it does not reach direct binder-aware petrography and its own table misstates NMR. The salt line (GEO-C003, GEO-C506; GEO-E004, GEO-E026) is a proponent report with no traced medieval source and an uncontrolled taste test against the wrong comparator. The Aswan material (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006) bears on the completeness of the pounding orthodoxy, not on casting. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is GEO-E020: without its positive control the Egyptian record would be two supportive and three negative studies with no demonstration that a casting signature is detectable at all, and the case would drift toward 'mixed'. With it, the Egyptian branch is contradicted in the tested recipe, and the case is unresolved only because the C–S–H variant and the Andean stone have never been independently examined.
assessment.steelman: The revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for. Every negative Egyptian study was built around Davidovits' alkali-aluminosilicate recipe; the one study with a positive control (GEO-E020) used an alkali geopolymer as that control and its author concedes a binder at about 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. Meanwhile GEO-E017 reports solid-state ²⁹Si/²⁷Al/⁴³Ca NMR on a Bent Pyramid casing stone reading as Tura grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel, GEO-E022 shows that lime plus diatomaceous earth forms exactly such a gel at room temperature from materials plausibly available in Egypt, and GEO-E012 reports Si–Ca–Mg ratios absent from all six candidate quarries. No published rebuttal of GEO-E017 exists. Add the proponents' scope restriction (casing, tops and backing blocks only, per GEO-E023) and the valid narrow form of GEO-C030 — quarry matching cannot see a binder — and a low-percentage lime-pozzolan cement in some casing stones is excluded by nothing in this ledger.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks produced on site by binding processed mineral inputs (geopolymer, natron/waterglass, lime-pozzolan, or related chemistry) rather than by carving natural rock alone. The two concrete instances are casing and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid and the andesite and sandstone blocks of Pumapunku/Tiwanaku.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether anomalies exist — a measured quarrying rate, salt reports, proponent SEM and NMR findings — but over three narrower things: whether the pro-casting laboratory results come from provenance-secure samples and survive independent replication; whether the negative petrography, built around an alkali recipe, also excludes the calcium-silicate binder the pro-casting side has moved to; and whether quarry-provenance matching, the strongest conventional evidence class, could detect casting at all if the aggregate came from the matched quarry.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For Egypt: an independent laboratory testing provenance-secure casing stone specifically for a calcium-silicate binder against matched Tura limestone, with criteria fixed in advance; and a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many blocks against a natural-limestone remanence baseline, which tests set-in-place versus quarried-and-rotated regardless of recipe. For the Andes: independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite, and a desk check of the Iwawe Stratum V deposit and the piedras cansadas against the excavators' own descriptions. Either direction is decisive for the specific monument.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Quarrying, carving, and transport with well-attested means: dolerite pounders and copper tools, fire-setting, ramps, sledges, levers, and large organized labor forces. This is supported by unfinished monuments abandoned mid-carve at quarries, tool marks and tools at extraction sites, worker settlements, experimental carving, and geochemical provenance matching such as Stone 58 to West Woods. Direct petrography of pyramid stone shows sedimentary bedding, fossils, and tectonic fractures that moulds do not produce; salt on interior walls has ordinary sources (efflorescence, groundwater, visitors); slow measured pounding rates imply more labour or supplementary techniques, not manufacture. The account's gaps are quantitative, not existential.

components.label: Great Pyramid blocks cast (GEO-C020)
components.note: Two supportive lab results (GEO-E012, GEO-E017), not independent of each other, with contested provenance; four negatives (GEO-E018–E021), one with a positive control. Contradicted for the alkali-geopolymer recipe; untested for the revised calcium-silicate binder.

components.label: Pumapunku/Tiwanaku blocks cast (GEO-C021, GEO-C004)
components.note: One proponent team, one contested sample set, never independently rerun; the only counter-evidence is a 1971 sandstone provenance study that does not address the andesite microscopy.

components.label: Feasibility and ingredients (GEO-C012, GEO-C010, GEO-C011, GEO-C013)
components.note: Natron supply is well documented and artificial limestone can be made; temperatures rest on priors more than ledger records; the fire-pit discovery story is a single unattributed anecdote. Necessary conditions, not evidence of occurrence.

components.label: Provenance-methods critique (GEO-C030)
components.note: Correct that PXRF/ICP-MS cannot see a binder and that quarry match is not proof of carving; wrong about NMR; does not reach the direct binder-aware petrography that examined the monument stone.

components.label: Aswan quarrying anomalies (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006)
components.note: One peer-reviewed rate measurement plus two unsurveyed proponent observations; all bear on the completeness of the pounding account, none on casting.

components.label: Salt and iconographic anchors (GEO-C003, GEO-C506, GEO-C005)
components.note: Salt report untraced to any medieval author; taste test uses the wrong comparator; mural reinterpretation is an unengaged proponent reading.

researchPriority.reason: Mainstream stakes are low, but the information gain per unit cost is unusually high: the Iwawe desk check, the salt-source trace, the halite comparator, and the provenance-methods audit are all cheap and each would move a featured claim decisively. The one expensive item — a blinded paleomagnetic or binder-specific test on provenance-secure pyramid stone — would be the first in-situ physical test that does not depend on disputed sample custody.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim is existential, so a single vindicated monument suffices and no number of natural monuments refutes it. The Egyptian instance has been tested directly and, in the recipe tested, contradicted (GEO-E018–E021), with GEO-E020's positive control showing the signature would have been visible. The Andean instance rests on one proponent team's results (GEO-E006, GEO-E007) never independently rerun. GEO-E009 undermines only the Stonehenge case and only through provenance. No monument has an independent positive result on provenance-secure samples; no independent negative exists for Pumapunku. That is a gap in testing, not an evidential tie.

treatment.plainLanguage: Somewhere, at least one great monument has blocks that were manufactured like concrete rather than cut from bedrock.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; every other claim matters only insofar as it moves this one.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every time monument stone has been examined directly by anyone outside the proponent camp it has read as natural, down to fossil worm tubes and calcite-filled tectonic fractures, and the one study with a positive control found no binder in any casing stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku organic and microstructural findings on provenance-secure andesite would move this toward provisionally_supported.
An independent lab finding a calcium-silicate cement in provenance-secure Great Pyramid casing stone absent from matched Tura limestone would do the same.
Independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy plus a targeted C–S–H test on casing stone returning nothing would move this to contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supportive: GEO-E012 (SEM/TEM microconstituents with Si–Ca–Mg ratios absent from six quarries; provenance contested by Egypt's antiquities authority) and GEO-E017 (NMR reading of a Bent Pyramid casing stone as Tura grains in a calcium-silicate gel; shares an author with GEO-E012). Undermining: GEO-E018 (macro sedimentary and tectonic features across many blocks in situ), GEO-E019 (Lauer sample natural, no zeolite cement), GEO-E021 (British Museum fragment natural; cristobalite is opal-CT), GEO-E020 (positive control shows alkali binder detectable and absent). GEO-E022 shows the revised binder is feasible, not that it was used. The alkali-geopolymer form is contradicted; the calcium-silicate form is untested; the sample-identity dispute over the Lauer piece is unresolved. Net: weak support in a narrow form.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the outer and upper blocks of the Great Pyramid are artificial limestone, set in place from a slurry.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The best-tested instance of the thesis; a clean positive or negative here would carry most of the case.
treatment.strongestObjection: Four independent petrographic examinations all conclude natural limestone, and Jana's side-by-side with a genuine geopolymer shows what casting looks like under the microscope and that no casing stone looks like it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A provenance-secure casing stone tested by an independent lab specifically for a C–S–H binder against matched Tura limestone, either way.

A blinded paleomagnetic survey of many blocks with a natural-limestone baseline: shared remanence aligned with the present field would force a mixed model; a null with adequate power would be the first in-situ negative independent of sample custody.
Resolution of the Lauer-sample identity dispute in either direction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supporting: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007, two peer-reviewed papers from one proponent team on one contested sample set, reporting SEM anomalies and organic matter in andesite. Undermining: GEO-E008, a 1971 provenance attribution of the red sandstones to natural quarries with pre-modern methods. The two lines address different lithologies and different questions, and neither has been independently replicated or re-examined. The proponents' own current model (natural Khapia andesite sand stored at Iwawe) concedes a Khapia origin, so provenance cannot separate the accounts; a lakeshore deposit and the piedras cansadas can, and that check has not been done.

treatment.plainLanguage: The famous H-blocks and sandstone slabs at Pumapunku were poured and set, not carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only branch where monument stone has been reported to show a casting signature; also the only one never checked by an outside laboratory.
treatment.strongestObjection: All laboratory support comes from the hypothesis's own principal proponents on samples whose chain of custody is disputed, and volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite on documented samples, either confirming the organics and microstructures or finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy.
The Iwawe Stratum V deposit described by its excavators as natural andesite sand (supports) or as dressing debris or unrelated fill (undermines).
Carved andesite ashlars documented in transit from Khapia would undermine wholesale casting regardless of the SEM findings.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E013 reports multi-ton demonstration blocks (self-reported, never independently analysed). GEO-E022 shows lime plus diatomaceous earth forms a C–S–H binder at room temperature. GEO-E012 is entered as support but its bearing is on occurrence, not feasibility. Indirectly, the genuine geopolymer limestone analysed in GEO-E020 is a real artificial limestone. Visual similarity to natural stone at monument scale has not been independently demonstrated.

treatment.plainLanguage: You can make hard, convincing artificial limestone blocks from ingredients and heat an ancient builder had.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary for the thesis but compatible with it being false; feasibility is not occurrence.
treatment.strongestObjection: The demonstration blocks are self-reported by the proponent institute, and modern production knowledge does not establish ancient production.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent analysis of a demonstration block confirming size, hardness, and visual similarity.
A documented failure to produce hard blocks at monument scale without modern reagents or equipment.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The ledger's only record is GEO-E016, a proponent citation of Badari-period glassmaking whose dating and temperature basis are unverified. The verdict leans on priors: copper metallurgy and glass and faience production in the ancient Near East are well established at these temperatures. What is not established is sustained industrial-scale heat of the kind stone-making at monument scale would need.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient furnaces with charcoal and bellows could reach the roughly 850 °C the natron chemistry needs.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An enabling condition; its truth barely moves the thesis and its falsity would kill only the natron route.
treatment.strongestObjection: Crucible-scale heat for glass beads is not the same as processing tonnes of reagent, and the ledger's own support is second-hand.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent verification of the Badari glass dating and firing temperatures.
Quantitative fuel-and-furnace estimates showing sustained 850 °C at the required throughput was infeasible.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010 (Shortland et al. 2006, strong) documents Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as the primary ancient natron sources with a decline and replacement by plant ash in the seventh to ninth centuries AD; GEO-E011 supplies the compositional criterion behind such timelines. Uncontroversial mainstream archaeology.

treatment.plainLanguage: Egypt had huge natural deposits of natron and used them for millennia, until the supply fell away in the early Middle Ages.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: True and irrelevant to whether any stone was cast; the natron papers concern glass and faience and say nothing about stone.
treatment.strongestObjection: None to the claim itself; the objection is to the inference from ingredient availability to use.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence that the documented natron supply was too small for anything beyond the vitreous industry would weaken the natron route's scale plausibility.

claimAssessments.reasoning: One record, GEO-E015: an unattributed anecdote recounted by a proponent, flagged as under-sourced in the project's own review, never replicated. Nothing contradicts it; nothing tests it.

treatment.plainLanguage: A campfire used for years could accidentally turn its ash into something like stone, showing how the idea might have been discovered.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An origin story; even if true it would not show any monument was cast, and if false casting could still have been discovered otherwise.
treatment.strongestObjection: An unattributed anecdote is not an observation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A controlled multi-month fire-pit replication producing (or failing to produce) structurally stone-like material.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E024 (moderate, qualifies) makes the narrow point correctly: PXRF and ICP-MS do not detect H, C, or O, and a quarry match constrains where the material came from, not how it was shaped; this legitimately qualifies GEO-E009. But the same record documents that Fóti's methods table misstates NMR, and GEO-E020 shows binder-aware petrography detects a casting signature when present, so the critique does not reach GEO-E018–E021. The claim is right about a class of methods and wrong as a general shield.

treatment.plainLanguage: Matching a stone's chemistry to a quarry can't tell you whether the stone was carved there or cast from that quarry's crushed rock, because the tests don't see the glue.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how much the strongest conventional evidence class constrains the thesis; does not itself provide any evidence for casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Direct microscopy and spectroscopy of monument stone — which the critique concedes exist — have been done, and found no binder.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A methods audit finding that major provenance studies did include binder-sensitive measurements would weaken the claim's practical force.
A demonstration that cast-from-aggregate stone shifts immobile-trace-element ratios enough to fail a quarry match would falsify the blindness premise.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 is a peer-reviewed photogrammetric measurement (216 cm³/h at 85 strikes/min) whose authors conclude against pounders as the sole method; single team, single granite and tool configuration, no replication. GEO-E002 supplies context on the thin Engelbach baseline, itself a proponent characterisation not yet checked against the monograph.

treatment.plainLanguage: When someone finally measured how fast a dolerite ball removes granite, it was very slow.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stresses the orthodox timeline; fully compatible with fire-setting, chisels, or more labour, and silent on casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Skilled ancient crews with maintained tools and fire-setting could far outperform one modern experimental protocol.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication with sensitivity to technique, tool mass, and granite type; a substantially higher rate would dissolve the anomaly.
Verification of Engelbach's actual trial against the 1922/1923 texts.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 is a proponent anecdote with no attempt counts, no effort quantification, and no survey of the test block; GEO-E002 is context only. Nothing contradicts it, but an unquantified absence is weak evidence of anything.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tourists have been hitting a granite test block with ancient pounders for decades and nobody has made a scoop mark.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Untrained visitors striking briefly is not a test of skilled quarrying; even if true it says nothing about casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Casual tourist strikes are not comparable to sustained skilled work, and no one has documented the block's wear either way.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A wear survey of the test block and a controlled skilled-pounding trial on the same granite.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005: a single proponent description of shaft dimensions and a biomechanical assertion, neither independently surveyed nor tested.

treatment.plainLanguage: Deep narrow shafts next to the obelisk seem too tight for anyone to swing a stone hammer at the bottom.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if the shafts are unpoundable, other extraction or drainage explanations exist; it does not point to casting specifically.
treatment.strongestObjection: The dimensions have not been measured by anyone without a stake in the answer, and shafts have prosaic quarrying uses.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent survey of shaft dimensions and tool-mark morphology at their bases.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E004 is the only record: the proponent institute's page recounts the report and Davidovits' own taste tests, and the primary Arabic sources remain untraced in this ledger. The claim is about what medieval accounts report; without a medieval author the ledger cannot say whether the report exists. Salt, if present, has mundane candidate origins.

treatment.plainLanguage: When a ninth-century caliph broke into the Great Pyramid, his men reportedly found the chamber walls crusted with salt.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a genuine medieval report of salt would be compatible with efflorescence from natural limestone, mortar, or groundwater; only bulk salt tied to the stone's chemistry would discriminate.
treatment.strongestObjection: The report has not been traced to any medieval source and comes from the hypothesis's own proponents.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Location of a credible primary Arabic account mentioning salt (supports) or a survey of the relevant accounts finding none (undermines).
Evidence that unworked Giza/Mokattam limestone effloresces halite naturally would make the report uninformative even if genuine.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E026 is an uncontrolled taste test on four visits with no instrument, no quantities, and a comparator (European cathedrals) that is the wrong control; the claim's assertion that comparable natural limestone lacks the salt has no comparator in the ledger at all. The record does not distinguish surface efflorescence from bulk salt.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pyramid stones taste salty and ordinary limestone buildings don't.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Surface salt cannot discriminate cast from natural stone; only bulk chlorine enrichment absent from matched bedrock would.
treatment.strongestObjection: The relevant comparator — unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock and quarry faces — has never been tested, and Giza limestone may carry halite natively.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: XRD of natural efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock alongside a chamber reference: halite present collapses the discriminator; halite absent makes the salt a genuine anomaly worth bulk testing.
Restoration and cleaning history of the chambers ruling modern contamination in or out.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 is an interpretive argument by a proponent; conventional Egyptology reads the scene as bronze casting and has not engaged the reinterpretation. No independent iconographic or inscriptional analysis is in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: A famous tomb painting of a big casting operation might show mineral processing rather than metalwork.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A picture cannot show what was in the crucibles; at best it would establish that large-scale casting operations were depicted.
treatment.strongestObjection: The scene's inscriptions and the conventional metallurgical reading have not been shown to fail; the reinterpretation is unengaged, not vindicated.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A joint Egyptological and history-of-technology re-examination of the mural and its inscriptions, with the residues and tools each reading predicts checked against the archaeological record.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The observation half is established: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 are peer-reviewed papers reporting organic matter and microstructural features in Pumapunku andesite. The interpretive half — that these are inconsistent with natural volcanic stone — rests on one team, one contested sample set, criteria never blind-tested, and no independent replication; volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally. Nothing in the ledger directly rebuts the measurements.

treatment.plainLanguage: Under the microscope, Pumapunku's andesite reportedly contains organic residue and textures its analysts say lava rock shouldn't have.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only laboratory evidence from a disputed monument that supports casting outright; its weight depends entirely on independence and sample custody.
treatment.strongestObjection: The findings come from the hypothesis's own proponents on samples of disputed provenance, and the criteria for 'inconsistent with natural stone' were never tested blind.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent re-analysis of documented Pumapunku andesite reproducing (or failing to reproduce) the organics and microstructures.
Blind testing of the discriminating criteria against undisputed natural andesite from Cerro Khapia.
